title: The potter's house (Jeremiah 18:1–6)
hookLine: clay spoiled on the wheel is shaped again
last: HERE, IN KITCHENS AND COURTS AND STREETS.

lines: GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.
A POT RISING ON THE WHEEL.
cards: "Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words." This time the message doesn't come in a vision or a dream. Jeremiah is sent on an errand, down to a workshop.
There's the potter, working a lump of clay at the wheel. Wet hands, a turning wheel, a pot rising. And then, halfway up, something goes wrong: a wobble, a slump, a wall caving in.
What the potter does next is the whole lesson.

teach.b: "And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it."

He doesn't throw the clay out, or sweep it off the wheel into the trash. The spoiled pot is still soft clay, and soft clay can be pressed back down and raised again into something else. Then the word comes.
"O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter?"

teach.h: AS CLAY IN THE POTTER'S HAND.
teach.b: And: "Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand."

teach.h: CLAY ON THE WHEEL CAN TURN.
teach.b: On its own, that could sound like a threat: you're just clay, and I can crush you. But read on. God says that if a nation he has spoken against turns from its evil, he will relent of the evil he planned for it.
And if a nation he planned to build turns to evil, the plan can change too. The potter image is about turning.
A vessel still on the wheel isn't finished; mistakes don't end it, they're the reason the potter's hands go back to work. Jewish tradition carries this picture into Yom Kippur.
In the Ashkenazi evening service, a liturgical poem built on Jeremiah's image is sung: behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so are we in your hand.
On the night of turning, the people call themselves clay that can still be reshaped.

how: On Yom Kippur evening, Ashkenazi prayer books include the liturgical poem Ki hineh kachomer, behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, which takes its image from Jeremiah 18.

games.q: you're the potter. the pot on your wheel slumps halfway up. what do you do?
o: press it down and make another vessel.
games.why: so he made it again another vessel: soft clay on the wheel can still be reshaped.

practice: Bring to mind one place that feels marred, a habit that slumped, a plan that caved in, a way you've been treating someone, and hold it the way a potter holds soft clay, without throwing it away or defending it.
Ask what it could become if it were pressed down and raised again. Then let your hands, your shoulders, your jaw go soft, like clay that can still move.
